research_rationale: EO 1547 (June 19, 1912, William H. Taft), read in full in the held ProQuest replica scan (archival_replica_scan_pending_codebook, acceptable_as_original false) and checked against the page image I rendered from the held PDF (sha256 2e446a81...; one page; printed number 'No. 1547', date 'June 19, 1912', signature 'Wm H Taft'). The OCR layer is complete; its errors ('I19' for 19, a stray apostrophe after 'hereby', '[No. 1547-.1') do not affect the operative words. Single operative command: under section 2 of the act of June 19, 1912 limiting the hours of daily service of laborers and mechanics on federal work (the 1912 eight-hour act), the act's provisions and stipulations 'are hereby waived, until January first, nineteen hundred and fifteen, as to any contract or contracts entered into in connection with the construction of the Isthmian Canal.' First end: by its own terms on 1915-01-01. Under the owner's 2026-10-21 ruling the 'until' date is inclusive, so the waiver runs through the end of January 1, 1915; the alternative exclusive reading is that it stopped when that day began, leaving December 31, 1914 as its last day. Authority check: no held source shows section 2 of the 1912 act repealed or amended before 1915; the held text of EO 2663 (1917, jobs/wikisource-texts/output/texts/EO_2663.txt) invokes section 2 of the same act (37 Stat. 137), which corroborates that the authority still existed after this order's end. The act's own effective-date clause is not held; it does not affect the end. The order states its own date, so its end does not depend on when the canal construction contracts were completed.
savings_reason: Contracts entered into while the waiver ran could lawfully omit the eight-hour stipulations, and work done under them was lawful. Where such a contract continued after January 1, 1915, its terms stood as made; that is an accrued effect of a contract formed under the waiver, carried by the contract and the 1912 act, and it does not keep the order operative, because the order commands nothing after its stated date. Pay for hours worked flows from the contracts and statute, not from the order. No held source shows any contract affected after 1915; this residual is a disclosed qualification, not a finding.
earlier_end_check: No earlier end is held. Candidates considered and not shown to extinguish the waiver: the Panama Canal Act of August 24, 1912 and EO 1885 (January 27, 1914, permanent organization of the Panama Canal) with EO 1888 (February 2, 1914, conditions of employment). The waiver attaches to contracts for canal construction, not to the Isthmian Canal Commission, and neither order's held summary or text names EO 1547 or the 1912 act's waiver; under the owner's rule a later general instrument ends a command only if something shows it extinguished that command, and nothing held does. The Panama Canal Act's text is not held. No extension: census titles, the WPA 1944 numbered list and the full text of all 2,750 ProQuest scan texts were searched on 2026-10-28 for Isthmian or Panama Canal orders touching eight-hour or hours-of-labor rules between 1912 and 1916; the only hits were EO 1547 itself, EO 2514 (January 15, 1917, Canal Zone leave rules, effective December 31, 1916) and EO 4459 (1926, Canal overtime pay), none of which names this waiver or acts before 1915. A citation search of every held order text for 'No. 1547' or 'Order 1547' found only Proclamation No. 1547 of 1919 (Scotts Bluff), a different instrument. The date is a fixed term of the waiver, not a deadline on another act.
scope_check: Whole order is one clause: a waiver for one class of contracts with one stated term. No partial amendment, extension or revocation of any part is held or found.
independent_command_check: No independent command survives. The recital of section 2 of the 1912 act is authority, not a command. The waiver has no proviso imposing a separate continuing duty.

research_rationale: EO 6663 (March 31, 1934), read in full in the held American Presidency Project transcription (two held copies of the same page, sha256 shared), exempts Luther L. Browning, linotype machinist in charge, Government Printing Office from section 204 of the Economy Act of June 30, 1932 and continues the employee in the service until April 1, 1935. Later orders further exempting the same person are held and added to this packet as source-supplement excerpts: EO 6984 (March 7, 1935) recites EO 6663 and further exempts Browning until April 1, 1936; EO 7307 (February 28, 1936) recites EO 6663 and EO 6984 and further exempts him until November 1, 1936. Each is recorded as a later event on the clause (clauses.csv). Extension reading, decided on the texts: each later order is a new exercise of the section 204 proviso with its own period. None says that the earlier order 'is amended' or alters its date; each recites the earlier exemption as a past grant ('who was exempted ... by Executive Order No. ...') and grants a further exemption 'until' a new date. EO 7645 confirms the reading by counting the earlier orders as separate 'periods totaling three years and eight months'. The strike-and-insert ruling does not apply because nothing is struck or inserted. So this order's own command ended on its own stated date, inclusive (exclusive alternative: ended when that day began), and each extension is recorded as a later event naming the same employee; the employee's exempt status continued without a gap under the extension orders. The alternative reading, that the extensions prolonged this order's command, would put its first end at the last extension's 'until' date (1936-11-01, inclusive); the texts do not support it, because no extension operates on this order's text. Legal reading: ends by its own terms on 1935-04-01, inclusive. The census, WPA and full-text name searches found no further order naming this person after the last extension. Authority: section 204 of Part II of the Legislative Appropriation Act of June 30, 1932 (47 Stat. 382, 404), whose proviso lets the President exempt a person from automatic separation at retirement age. No held source shows section 204 repealed or amended before this order's stated end. research_rationale: EO 6874 (October 16, 1934, Franklin D. Roosevelt), read in full in the held American Presidency Project transcription. It is not a closing order (the type label closing_mourning is wrong; the WPA 1944 list, 1935 CSR 28, and the APP title agree): under the Civil Service Act of January 16, 1883 it amends paragraph 6 of subdivision VII of schedule A of the civil-service rules 'to read as follows': '6. Temporary clerks, carriers, and laborers required for part-time or intermittent work in the Postal Service in connection with the present holiday or seasonal business from this date to February 1, 1935.' Decision on its own terms. The order's one command is the rewrite of paragraph 6; under the strike-and-insert ruling the rewritten paragraph is the operative clause and continues, amended, until something ends it. Two candidate ends exist in held evidence. (a) The inserted text's own period: the paragraph excepts positions only 'from this date to February 1, 1935'. That period is part of the exception's definition, so after February 1, 1935 the paragraph excepted no position; the text itself is the evidence that its operation ended, and nothing held extended it (the WPA 1944 list shows no amendment of subdivision VII paragraph 6 between October 16, 1934 and October 19, 1935). (b) EO 7209 (October 19, 1935; held government-printed text, added here as SUPPLEMENT:EO7209) amends paragraph 6 'to read as follows' with a new period to February 1, 1936; its words show it replaced the paragraph's text, but by then the 1934 exception had already stopped operating. Conclusion: the clause terminated by its own terms on 1935-02-01, read inclusively (exclusive alternative: it stopped when that day began, so January 31, 1935 was its last day); EO 7209's replacement of the spent text on 1935-10-19 is recorded as a later event, not as the end. Under the evidence-decides ruling EO 7209 is not a default end, and here the earlier own-terms end is evidenced. Savings: appointments made under the exception during its period are accrued; they do not keep the exception operative. Earlier versions of paragraph 6 (EO 5731, 1931; EO 5930, 1932; EO 6352, 1933) precede this order and do not affect its end.

research_rationale: EO 7208 (October 19, 1935), read in full in the held American Presidency Project transcription (two held copies of the same page, sha256 shared), exempts George G. Hedgcock, senior pathologist, Bureau of Plant Industry, Agriculture from section 204 of the Economy Act of June 30, 1932 and continues the employee in the service until November 1, 1936. Identity: number, date, person and title agree across the APP page, the census register and the WPA 1944 numbered list. The order recites EO 6338 (October 14, 1933) and EO 6862 (September 30, 1934), recited earlier exemptions. Later orders further exempting the same person are held and added to this packet as source-supplement excerpts: EO 7475 (October 19, 1936) recites EO 6338, 6862 and 7208 and further exempts Hedgcock until July 1, 1937; EO 7645 (June 24, 1937) recites EO 6338, 6862, 7208 and 7475 ("periods totaling three years and eight months") and further exempts him until January 1, 1938. Each is recorded as a later event on the clause (clauses.csv). Extension reading, decided on the texts: each later order is a new exercise of the section 204 proviso with its own period. None says that the earlier order 'is amended' or alters its date; each recites the earlier exemption as a past grant ('who was exempted ... by Executive Order No. ...') and grants a further exemption 'until' a new date. EO 7645 confirms the reading by counting the earlier orders as separate 'periods totaling three years and eight months'. The strike-and-insert ruling does not apply because nothing is struck or inserted. So this order's own command ended on its own stated date, inclusive (exclusive alternative: ended when that day began), and each extension is recorded as a later event naming the same employee; the employee's exempt status continued without a gap under the extension orders. The alternative reading, that the extensions prolonged this order's command, would put its first end at the last extension's 'until' date (1938-01-01, inclusive); the texts do not support it, because no extension operates on this order's text. Legal reading: ends by its own terms on 1936-11-01, inclusive. The census, WPA and full-text name searches found no further order naming this person after the last extension.
